instructions.content: Search is discovery, not analysis: the goal is a structured candidate list.
ALWAYS add a short delay between batch calls: without an API key the limit is 3 req/s, and bulk PMID fetches without a delay cause silent failures or 429s.
ALWAYS check whether a PubTator or PubMed MCP is configured before invoking the Python script.
NEVER attempt to download a PDF without first confirming PMC availability and open-access status.
If a PubTator or PubMed MCP is configured and reachable, prefer it over the script.
Set up the environment on first run (create the venv and install dependencies) as described in the setup reference.
Choose the subcommand that fits the task: search (--keywords, or --term with author, journal and date filters), metadata, analyze, download; --show-abstract gives a richer preview.
If the script returns HTTP 429, wait 30 s and retry once.
NEVER retry in a tight loop on 429; if still failing, set PUBMED_API_KEY or switch to the MCP.
NEVER triage automatically: present the candidates and ALWAYS confirm with the user before handing off to triage-paper.
NEVER hardcode API keys in scripts or task files; ALWAYS use environment variables (PUBMED_API_KEY) or a gitignored dotenv file.
NEVER treat abstract-based analysis as a full-text review; qualify it as abstract-based and recommend obtaining the full text.
Do not use this skill when the paper is already known by DOI or URL; go straight to triage-paper.
Reuse an existing candidate JSON at /tmp/<topic>-candidates.json instead of searching again.
Use google-scholar-search or semantic-scholar-search for general academic literature rather than PubMed.
Export candidate lists with --format json and --output so they can be reused.
